analogy.p: Engineers testing a bridge check each beam as it is built (iterative testing), then test the finished bridge with a heavy load (final testing). They test normal traffic (normal data), the maximum weight limit and one tonne over it (boundary data), and absurd loads that should be refused outright (invalid and erroneous data), and they decide in advance what must happen in each case (the test plan). The analogy breaks down because a bridge is tested once by physical load, whereas a program can be run unlimited times cheaply with automated test data, and a software fix can accidentally break other parts.

bullets: Purpose of testing: to check that a program **works as intended** and meets its requirements.
Two stages: **iterative** testing (while developing) and **final / terminal** testing (at the end).
Test data types: **normal, boundary, invalid and erroneous**.
Use a **test plan** with expected results decided before running the tests.
Use the results to **find errors and refine the algorithm or code**, then retest.
Links to **types of error** (syntax and logic) in the next specification point.
Often asked together with **validation**: you test a validation routine using all types of test data.
core.p: The OCR J277 specification (2.3.2) expects you to understand the **purpose of testing**, the difference between **iterative testing** and **final (terminal) testing**, how to **identify and fix errors**, and how to **select and use suitable test data**: normal, boundary and invalid or erroneous data. You may be asked to explain these ideas, to choose test data for a given program, to complete a test plan, or to state which kind of test data a value is. This topic is heavily examined because it can be asked about almost any program in Paper 2.

bullets: **To find errors** (bugs) in the program so they can be fixed.
To check the program **meets the user's requirements** and works as intended.
To check it **does not crash** or give wrong results with unusual input (robustness).
To make sure that **every route** through the program (every branch of an IF, every loop) works.
To give **confidence** to the client that the program can be released.
Testing finds the **presence** of errors, not their absence: a test that passes does not prove all inputs work.
Bugs found early are **cheaper and easier** to fix than those found after release.
core.p: Testing is the process of running a program with chosen inputs to check whether it behaves correctly. Its main purpose is to **find errors** so that they can be corrected before the software is used. It also shows whether the program meets the requirements set out at the start, whether it is robust (copes with unexpected input without crashing) and whether it gives the correct output for every kind of input. Testing can show that errors exist, but no amount of testing can prove that a program has no errors at all, so the aim is to choose tests that are as thorough as possible.

bullets: Carried out **during** development, repeatedly, after each part is written.
The programmer **tests each module/subprogram** on its own before combining them.
Errors are found **early**, when they are small and easy to locate.
Fixes are made **before** more code depends on the faulty part.
Often done by the **programmer** using their own test data.
Tools such as the **IDE debugger** (breakpoints, stepping, variable watch) are used.
Links to **modular programming**: small subprograms are much easier to test iteratively.
core.p: **Iterative testing** is testing that is carried out repeatedly **during development**. As each module, subprogram or section of the program is completed it is tested straight away, errors are fixed, and only then does the programmer move on and build more on top. Because each test covers only a small part, any error found must be in the code written most recently, so it is much quicker to locate. Iterative testing goes hand in hand with writing the program in small modules and uses tools such as breakpoints, stepping through code and trace tables to follow what the code does.

bullets: Done at the **end**, on the **complete program**, with all modules joined.
Checks the program **meets the original requirements** (the specification).
Finds problems in how **modules interact**, which iterative tests may miss.
Uses a full **test plan** covering normal, boundary and invalid or erroneous data.
Often includes **realistic data** and may involve the end users or client.
If errors are found the program is **fixed and retested**.
Final testing happens **after** iterative testing; it does not replace it.
core.p: **Final testing**, also called **terminal testing**, takes place at the **end** of development when the whole program has been completed and all the parts are put together. The program is tested as a complete system to check that it meets the requirements agreed at the start and that the parts work correctly together. Parts that worked perfectly alone can still fail when combined, for example if one module passes data in the wrong format to another. Final testing is often carried out with realistic data, sometimes by the client or users.

bullets: **When**: iterative = during development; final = at the end of development.
**What is tested**: iterative = a module or section; final = the whole program.
**Purpose**: iterative = find and fix errors as you go; final = check the complete program meets requirements.
**Cost of errors**: iterative errors are easier and cheaper to find; final errors may be harder to trace.
**Repeated?** Iterative testing is repeated many times; final testing is done once the program is complete (and again after fixes).
Both use **test data** and a **test plan**.
Mark scheme words: 'during development' versus 'at the end / on the completed program'.
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare the two. The easiest way to remember the difference is **when** and **what**: iterative testing happens during development on individual parts, while final testing happens at the end on the whole program. Both are needed. Iterative testing keeps errors small and local, and final testing confirms that the finished product does what the client wanted.

bullets: Valid data that **should be accepted** and processed.
Lies **inside** the allowed range or format, not on the edge.
Example: age check 11 to 18, normal data = **14**.
Example: password length 8 to 12, normal data = a **10-character** password.
Expected result is **correct output / data accepted**, not an error message.
Choose **more than one** normal value if different paths exist in the program.
Normal data shows the program works **under typical use**.
core.p: **Normal data** is data that the program is designed to accept and that falls comfortably inside the valid range. It is the type of data a typical user would enter, so testing with normal data checks that the program works correctly in everyday use. For a range check of ages 11 to 18, normal test data could be 14 or 16. The expected result is that the data is accepted and processed correctly. A test plan should include several different normal values, to cover different paths through the program.

bullets: Tests the **limits** of the valid range.
Valid boundaries: lowest and highest allowed values, e.g. **11 and 18**; these should be **accepted**.
Just outside the boundary: **10 and 19**; these should be **rejected**.
Catches **off-by-one** errors, such as writing < 18 instead of <= 18.
Applies to numbers, lengths of strings, and number of loop repeats.
Example: discount from £50: test **49.99 and 50**.
Always say what **each** boundary value should do (accepted or rejected).
core.p: **Boundary data** is data **at the very edge** of what is allowed, because programming errors often occur at limits, for example using greater than instead of greater than or equal to. To test a boundary you use the **highest and lowest valid values** and the values **just outside** them. For ages 11 to 18 the boundaries are 11 and 18 (valid and accepted) and 10 and 19 (just outside, rejected). Testing at both sides of each limit shows that the comparison operators and loops are correct.

bullets: **Invalid**: right type, outside the allowed range, e.g. **25 or -3** for an age of 11 to 18.
**Erroneous**: wrong data type, e.g. **abc, 4.5 or an empty input** where an integer is expected.
Expected outcome: data is **rejected** with an **error message**; the program **does not crash**.
Tests the **validation** routines (range, type, length, presence, format checks).
Link: each validation check should be tested with **all kinds** of test data.
Include **different types** of bad data: too high, too low, wrong type, blank.
State in the exam whether data should be **accepted or rejected**.
core.p: **Invalid data** is data of the correct type that falls **outside** what the program should accept, such as an age of 25 when only 11 to 18 is allowed. **Erroneous data** is data of the **wrong type or format** altogether, such as the word abc where a number is expected. Some mark schemes combine them as invalid/erroneous, and some use erroneous to mean data that should be rejected. In both cases the expected result is the same: the program should **reject** the data with a suitable message and **not crash**.

bullets: Columns: **test no., purpose, test data, expected result, actual result, pass/fail**.
Expected results must be **worked out before** running the program.
Cover **normal, boundary and invalid/erroneous** data.
Number the tests so a failed test can be **retested** after the fix.
If **actual differs from expected**, there is an error to find and correct.
Keeping the plan gives **evidence** that testing was thorough.
Mark schemes reward **specific, different** test values and **precise expected results**.
core.p: A **test plan** is a table drawn up **before** the tests are run. Each row has a test number, the purpose of the test, the test data, the **expected result** and later the **actual result**, with pass or fail. Deciding the expected result in advance is essential, otherwise you cannot tell whether the program is correct. A good plan covers every type of test data and every path through the program. After each run the actual result is compared with the expected one: if they differ there is an error to investigate.

bullets: **Syntax error**: breaks the language rules (misspelt keyword, missing bracket); the program will not run.
**Logic error**: the program runs but gives **wrong output** (wrong operator, wrong condition).
Compare **actual with expected** results to find which tests failed.
Use **trace tables**, breakpoints and stepping through the code to locate the fault.
Fix the code and then **rerun the test** that failed.
Types of error are covered in more detail in the next specification point.
Syntax errors are found by the **translator**; logic errors are found by **testing**.
core.p: When a test fails, the programmer must find the cause and fix it. The J277 course describes two main types of error: a **syntax error** breaks the rules of the language, so the program cannot run at all, and a **logic error** lets the program run but produce the wrong result, for example using the wrong operator. Finding logic errors is where thorough test data and debugging tools matter most, and a trace table lets you follow the values of variables step by step to see where the output goes wrong.

bullets: After a failure, **change the code or algorithm**, then **retest**.
Retest the **failed test** and the **earlier tests**: a fix can break something that worked.
Refining can also mean making the code **more robust** or easier to maintain.
The cycle **repeats until all tests pass**.
Keep the **test plan** up to date with any new tests.
Link to **iterative development** and **maintainability**.
Final testing should be repeated after significant changes.
core.p: Testing is not finished when a fault is found. The programmer **refines** the algorithm or code to correct the fault, improve it or make it more robust, then runs the tests again. Fixing one error can accidentally introduce another, so after every change the earlier tests should be repeated as well as the one that failed. This cycle of write, test, find errors, fix and retest continues until all tests give the expected result.

bullets: Identify the **range or rule** first: write down valid and invalid values before choosing.
Give **actual values**, not descriptions such as 'a number too high'.
For a boundary question, give **both sides** of the edge.
State the **expected outcome** for each value: accepted, rejected or the calculated result.
For **calculation** programs, check your expected result by hand.
Do not repeat the **same type** of data and expect extra marks.
Link testing to **validation**: test data is chosen to check each validation rule.
core.p: Exam questions test this topic in four main ways. You may be asked to **define** terms like iterative testing, to **state** the type of a given test value, to **choose** suitable test data for a described program, or to **complete a test plan**. The marks come from precise values and clear expected results, not general statements. Always use numbers from the question rather than vague descriptions, and write the expected result for every test.

exam: Typical marks: **1** to name or define a test type, **2** to describe, **4** to choose test data or complete a test plan, up to **6** for discussing testing.
For **iterative vs final**: always say 'during development' for iterative and 'at the end / whole program' for final.
For test data questions: write **real values** and say whether each is **normal, boundary or invalid/erroneous**.
Give **expected results** with every value, using the exact wording of the question: accepted, rejected, error message, or a calculated value.
For a **range** (a to b): normal inside, boundary **a and b** (plus just outside), invalid outside, erroneous wrong type.
For a **length** check (e.g. 8 to 12 characters): count characters carefully; check your test strings are the stated length.
In a **test plan table**, fill in the columns exactly as asked; do not leave expected results blank.
For '**why test**' questions: 'to find errors', 'to check the program works as intended / meets requirements', 'so errors can be fixed'.
Do not say testing 'makes the program perfect'; say it **finds errors** so they can be fixed.
Link to **validation** when relevant: test data should check every validation rule works.

mistakes.r: Boundary data tests the limits of the range: both the lowest and highest valid values and the values just outside them.
mistakes.w: Boundary data is the highest value allowed only.

mistakes.r: Normal data is valid data within the allowed range that the program should accept.
mistakes.w: Normal data is any data I like.

mistakes.r: Invalid and erroneous data should be rejected, with an error message, without the program crashing.
mistakes.w: Invalid and erroneous data should be accepted by the program.

mistakes.r: Testing can show the presence of errors but cannot prove there are none.
mistakes.w: Testing proves a program has no errors.

mistakes.r: Give an actual value, such as 25, and state the expected result (rejected).
mistakes.w: Giving test data as 'a number that is too high'.

mistakes.r: Each test needs an expected result worked out in advance, so it can be compared with the actual result.
mistakes.w: Not stating expected results in a test plan.

mistakes.r: Iterative testing happens during development; final testing happens at the end.
mistakes.w: Iterative testing happens after the program is finished.

mistakes.r: Test both sides of each boundary, for example 18 (accepted) and 19 (rejected).
mistakes.w: Only testing for the one boundary value.

summary: The specification asks you to know why programs are tested, the difference between iterative and final (terminal) testing, and how to choose and use normal, boundary and invalid or erroneous test data in a test plan to find and fix errors. It matters because testing questions appear regularly in Paper 2 and need precise values and expected results.

terms.d: Running a program with chosen data to check that it works as intended and to find errors.
Testing carried out repeatedly during development, on each module or section as it is written.
Testing carried out at the end of development on the complete program (also called terminal testing).
A table of planned tests with test data and expected results, completed with actual results when tests are run.
The values chosen to be entered into a program during testing.
Valid data that the program should accept, within the expected range.
Data at the edge of the allowed range, including the values just outside it.
Data of the correct type that is outside the allowed range and should be rejected.
Data of the wrong type or format that should be rejected by the program.
The outcome the program should produce for a test, decided before the test is run.
The outcome that the program really produces when the test is run.
An error that breaks the rules of the programming language so the program cannot run.
An error that lets the program run but gives an incorrect result.
A table used to record the values of variables as each line of an algorithm is followed.
Finding and removing errors from a program.
Able to cope with unexpected or incorrect input without crashing.

worked.ans: Normal: 14, accepted. Boundary: 18, accepted (also 11 accepted; 10 and 19 rejected). Invalid: 25, rejected with an error message (erroneous data such as abc would also be rejected).
worked.q: A program asks the user to enter an age. The age must be from 11 to 18 inclusive. Give one example of normal, boundary and invalid test data and state the expected result for each. [6]
steps: Boundary: 18 (or 11, 10 or 19) (1), expected: accepted if 11 or 18 and rejected if 10 or 19 (1).
Invalid: 25 (outside range) (1), expected: rejected with an error message (1).

worked.q: A shop gives a 10% discount when the total is £50 or more. Complete a test plan with four tests using normal and boundary data, with the expected result for each. [4]
steps: Normal below the limit: total 30, no discount, pay 30.00 (1).
Boundary just below: 49.99, no discount, pay 49.99 (1).
Boundary on the limit: 50, discount applied, 50 x 0.9 = 45.00 (1).
Normal above the limit: 80, discount applied, 80 x 0.9 = 72.00 (1).

worked.ans: Any two of: pass1234 (8 characters) accepted; password1234 (12 characters) accepted; pass123 (7 characters) rejected; password12345 (13 characters) rejected.
worked.q: A password must be 8 to 12 characters long. Give test data for two boundary tests and state the expected results. [4]
steps: Valid lower boundary: pass1234 has 8 characters, expected accepted (1 mark for value, 1 for expected result together).
Just outside the lower boundary: pass123 has 7 characters, expected rejected.
Valid upper boundary: password1234 has 12 characters, expected accepted.
Just outside the upper boundary: password12345 has 13 characters, expected rejected.
